extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning how to write proofs and disproofs
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidelines for producing and evaluating mathematical proofs and disproofs, including counterexamples, direct/contrapositive/contradiction methods, induction (ordinary and strong), and smallest-counterexample arguments. Geared to exercises that ask 'prove or disprove' and to constructing rigorous inductive proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove a statement by proving its negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P, prove ¬P. In other words, to show P is false, prove that its negation is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proof of ¬P can be carried out by direct proof, contrapositive, or contradiction. The text summarizes the approach succinctly: 'How to disprove P: Prove ∼P.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove universally quantified statements using counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∀ x ∈ S, P(x), produce an example x ∈ S for which P(x) is false, since ¬(∀x P(x)) = ∃x ¬P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Produce an example of an x ∈ S that makes P(x) false.' Example: showing f(11) = 121 demonstrates the falsehood of 'for every n, f(n) is prime.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove conditional statements by exhibiting a counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P(x) ⇒ Q(x), produce an x for which P(x) is true and Q(x) is false (this yields a counterexample to the universal conditional claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Produce an example of an x that makes P(x) true and Q(x) false.' This is the conditional analog of the universal counterexample strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain explicitly how a counterexample makes the statement false
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting a counterexample, you must show concretely how it violates the statement (not merely assert 'consider n = ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For instance, after choosing n = 11 to disprove a primality conjecture, demonstrate f(11) = 121 = 11·11 to show it is not prime. The text warns that simply naming the example without justification is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove existence statements by proving the universal negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove ∃ x ∈ S, P(x), prove ¬(∃x P(x)) = ∀ x ∈ S, ¬P(x); that is, show for every x in S that P(x) is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the negation is universally quantified, a single counterexample does not suffice. Use direct proof, contrapositive, or contradiction to show ¬P(x) holds for all x. Example: the claim 'there exists x with x^4 < x < x^2' is disproved by proving for all real x this cannot hold (done via contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproof by contradiction (outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove P using contradiction: assume P is true and deduce a contradiction, thereby concluding P is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline given: 'Assume P is true, and deduce a contradiction.' The text illustrates with the x^4 < x < x^2 example by assuming existence and deriving an impossible inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the three major proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary methods of proving statements are direct proof, contrapositive proof, and proof by contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book repeatedly uses these methods across examples; choosing the appropriate one depends on the form of the statement (e.g., existence vs. universal vs. conditional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by (simple) mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove all Sn (n = 1,2,3,...): (1) prove the base case S1 (basis step); (2) for arbitrary k ≥ 1, prove Sk ⇒ Sk+1 (inductive step). Conclude every Sn holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inductive step is typically done by assuming Sk (the inductive hypothesis) and using it in a direct proof to establish Sk+1. The 'domino' analogy is used to explain the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive hypothesis usage and base index flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In the inductive step assume the statement at the current index (Sk) to prove the next (Sk+1); the base case need not be S1 — it can be S0 or Sm depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the basis step to the smallest relevant index. The text emphasizes that basis is usually simple but may be S0 or another starting integer depending on the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about the domain of induction (limitations for integers beyond the base)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard induction from a base (e.g., S1 and Sk ⇒ Sk+1) only establishes Sn for n ≥ base; it does not prove statements for indices less than the base (e.g., negative integers) unless additional implications are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove ∀ n ∈ Z you'd need to show extra implications (e.g., Sk ⇒ Sk−1) or establish base cases and implications that cover the intended index set. The text warns that induction does not automatically cover S0, S−1, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove S1, S2, ... by strong induction: (1) prove base statement(s) (possibly several); (2) for arbitrary k ≥ base, assume S1 ∧ S2 ∧ ... ∧ Sk and prove Sk+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong induction lets you use all prior cases up to k in proving the (k+1)th case. The basis may require checking multiple initial statements (e.g., S8,S9,S10 for the postage example).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction (diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when Sk alone does not easily imply Sk+1 but some earlier Sm (m < k) or several earlier cases together will imply Sk+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: postage problem (need S8–S10 in basis because proving Sk+1 uses Sk−2), and proving 12 | (n^4 − n^2) where multiple base cases up to 6 are checked and Sk−5 ⇒ Sk+1 is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by smallest counterexample (hybrid induction/contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove all Sn: (1) show S1 (or base) true; (2) assume some Sn is false; (3) let k be the smallest index with Sk false; (4) use truth of Sk−1 (and structure) to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method forces a point where a true and false case collide (Sk−1 true and Sk false) and uses that to derive a contradiction; example given: proving 4 | (5^n − 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction with additional variables: prove uniformly over other parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: When Sn involves another variable (e.g., P(n,x) for all x in some set), the base and inductive steps must hold for all values of that variable in its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bernoulli's inequality (1 + x)^n ≥ 1 + nx must be shown for all x > −1 in both base and inductive steps; one proves the induction hypothesis 'for all x in domain' and then multiplies by (1+x) etc., taking care about sign conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality-manipulation guideline used in induction proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: You may add unequal quantities to both sides of an inequality provided you add a larger quantity to the larger side (or ensure monotonicity conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights this oft-neglected fact with: if x ≤ y and a ≤ b then x + a ≤ y + b; and uses it in an induction step (e.g., in the inequality 2^n ≤ 2^{n+1} − 2^{n−1} − 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural reduction in inductive proofs (reduce to smaller instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many inductive proofs, reduce the object to smaller instances (e.g., remove an edge from a tree producing two smaller trees) and apply the inductive hypothesis to those pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving 'a tree with n vertices has n−1 edges' by removing an edge to get two smaller trees with x and y vertices, applying the hypothesis to each, and recombining counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine proof techniques for existence and uniqueness (e.g., Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex existence/uniqueness theorems may require combining strong induction, cases, and minimal-counterexample reasoning: use strong induction to prove existence of a prime factorization and other techniques (e.g., uniqueness arguments) to show uniqueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text outlines proving existence of prime factorizations by strong induction (if n+1 is composite, factor into a·b and apply hypothesis to a and b) and indicates uniqueness is handled by further argumentation possibly using minimal-counterexample ideas.
